name: fast-float (Rust port of fast_float)
baseline: strtod from the C standard library (also compared: abseil C++, netlib C, fast_float C++)
workload: Parse one decimal string into a 64-bit float; best timing in ns per number on the canada, mesh, uniform, iidi, iei and rec32 datasets.
claimed_speedup: README tables, ns per number, fast-float vs strtod (C): Intel i7-4771 canada 21.58 vs 286.10, uniform 19.36 vs 258.73, mesh 10.70 vs 31.15; Apple M1 canada 14.84 vs 176.13, uniform 11.24 vs 165.43; AMD Rome canada 25.90 vs 123.37, uniform 20.54 vs 101.58, mesh 12.12 vs 65.68 (ratios of roughly 2.9x to 13x across all datasets, derived from page data). README text: 2-8x faster than Rust std FromStr, about 2-3x faster than the nearest competitors, and within noise of the original fast_float C++ library.
compiler_and_flags: Rust 1.49; crate release profile sets lto = "fat", codegen-units = 1. Compiler and flags for the C and C++ rows are not stated (they come from lemire/simple_fastfloat_benchmark).
hardware: Intel i7-4771 3.5GHz (macOS), Apple M1 (macOS), AMD Rome (Linux)
why_faster: Direct port of Lemire's fast_float (Eisel-Lemire method): a fast path for inputs with at most 19 significant digits and a slower exact path for longer ones; the C strtod row uses a general arbitrary-precision approach (the second half is this agent's inference, the README names only the fast-path design).
tradeoffs: Parses decimal text to f32/f64 only (no formatting). No dependencies, no_std capable. Repo last committed July 2021 (crate 0.2.0 from January 2021).
caveats: The algorithm is Lemire's, already catalogued as fast_float (C++); the Rust port matches it within noise, so the win over strtod is algorithmic rather than a language advantage. Benchmarks are first-party, the Rust version is 1.49 and compiler flags for the C rows are missing, so the tier is C. The strtod row is whatever libc the machine had: macOS libc on the Intel and M1 rows, and (not stated, presumably glibc) on AMD Rome. Newer Rust standard-library releases may have narrowed the from_str gap (not checked this session). Included mainly as the Rust-side evidence for the algorithm.
found_via: GitHub: topics/string-search and WebFetch of aldanor/fast-float-rust while checking Rust numeric-text crates against C libc functions

name: sliceslice (Rust SIMD substring search)
baseline: sse4-strstr avx2_strstr_v2 (C++ SIMD substring search by Wojciech Mula); also compared against Rust std String::find, memmem and twoway crates. Not compared against glibc memmem/strstr or std::string::find.
workload: Single-pattern substring search with AVX2 over a short haystack and a long haystack (bench/benches/i386.rs); total time in ms.
claimed_speedup: README table, ms [mid]: long haystack sliceslice DynamicAvx2Searcher 35.181 vs sse4-strstr avx2_strstr_v2 (C++) 38.579 (about 1.10x, derived from page data) and vs Rust std String::find 345.01; short haystack sliceslice 79.416 vs sse4-strstr 75.515 (sse4-strstr is about 5% faster there).
compiler_and_flags: gcc 9.3.0 (flags not stated) for sse4-strstr; Rust 1.46.0 (flags not stated)
why_faster: README: SIMD-accelerated single-pattern search based on Wojciech Mula's generic SIMD algorithm; the same algorithm is what sse4-strstr implements, so the difference is implementation detail, not stated by the source.
tradeoffs: x86 AVX2 (runtime-dispatched searcher types) rather than portable; sliceslice itself is memory safe, unlike sse4-strstr, which can read beyond the end of the haystack (README footnote). Single needle per searcher.
caveats: Weak claim: the only C/C++ row is a research SIMD routine (not glibc or libstdc++), the margin is 10% on long haystacks and a loss on short ones, and the toolchains are from 2020 (Rust 1.46). memchr's memmem (already catalogued in the wave papers file) is the stronger Rust result against glibc. Included so the verifier can decide whether a research-routine baseline counts.
found_via: WebSearch: 'Rust crate substring search SIMD faster than glibc memmem strstr benchmark libc' led to docs.rs/sliceslice; opened github.com/cloudflare/sliceslice-rs

name: zog (Zig SIMD JSONL search)
baseline: jq (C); the README row is labelled 'jq/jaq' so it is not clear which of the two produced each number; ripgrep (Rust) is also compared
workload: Search, filter, extract and aggregate over a 1 GB JSONL file with 6.7 million lines; GB/s per workload.
claimed_speedup: README: '20-50x faster than jq/jaq for typical queries'; table, GB/s zog(file) / ripgrep / jq-jaq: simple key match 4.03 / 2.30 / 0.07, substring match 2.49 / 1.53 / 0.07, numeric comparison 3.39 / 2.97 / 0.10, aggregations 2.41 / N/A / 0.05, complex logic 2.24 / 0.54 / 0.06. Also 'faster than ripgrep for all matching categories'.
compiler_and_flags: zig build -Doptimize=ReleaseFast (build instructions); no flags given for the benchmarks or the baselines
hardware: Only 'a modern NVMe SSD' is named; no CPU model
why_faster: Repository description: zero-allocation JSONL search engine using SIMD (field matching without building a DOM); jq parses every line into a full value tree. Mechanism is from the repo description, not from a profile.
tradeoffs: Query language is limited to the supported match, extract and aggregate forms; it is a filter tool, not a general jq replacement.
caveats: First-party only: no CPU, no benchmark script path, no baseline versions or flags, and the jq and jaq numbers are merged into one column. Different work is being compared (SIMD key scan versus full JSON parse), so this is a tool-versus-tool result and not a language comparison. JSONL tools are a JSON-category topic as much as a text one.

name: Whichlang (Rust language detection)
baseline: CLD 2 (Google Compact Language Detector 2, C++; the Lingua README lists it among Rust-ecosystem options via the rust-cld2 bindings, so the row presumably runs the C++ code through FFI); Whatlang (Rust) is also compared
workload: Time to classify 2,000 sentences in the 16 languages that every detector supports (single thread and multi-thread), plus a script timing 3,000 texts per supported language.
claimed_speedup: Lingua README 'How fast is it?': Whichlang 4.47 ms vs CLD 2 23.92 ms single thread (about 5.4x, derived from page data) and 651.89 us vs 4.81 ms multi thread (about 7.4x, derived); accuracy-script run time Whichlang 0.28 s vs CLD 2 1.70 s (about 6.1x, derived). Whichlang's own README only compares with Whatlang (about 10x faster; 0.26 us vs 16.62 us on short text) and claims above 100 MB/s throughput.
compiler_and_flags: Not stated ('cargo bench --features benchmark' in the Lingua repository)
hardware: iMac 3.6 GHz 8-core Intel Core i9 with 40 GB RAM (stated for the Lingua README table)
why_faster: Whichlang README: a small multiclass logistic regression over hashed 2-4-gram letter and codepoint features projected into a 4,096-dimension space (the hashing trick), with no dependencies. Whatlang's comparison table lists CLD2 as quadgram based; the link between model size and speed is this agent's inference.
tradeoffs: Supports only 16 languages (CLD2 supports about 83 per the Whatlang README table); the author reports 99.5% accuracy on a private validation set, and accuracy is lower for short inputs. No HTML handling.
caveats: The CLD2 comparison is in a competitor's README (Lingua), not in Whichlang's own, and compiler flags and CLD2 build details are not given. The test is restricted to the 16 common languages, which favours the small model. Whichlang's accuracy against CLD2 is not shown on the page I opened. Whatlang, the other Rust detector in the table, is slower than CLD2 single-threaded (36.24 ms vs 23.92 ms), so this is a Whichlang result, not a Rust-versus-C++ one.

name: stepreduce-rs (Rust port of stepreduce)
baseline: stepreduce C++ original (uses libstdc++ std::regex) by Seth Hillbrand
workload: Lossless size reduction of one 1 MiB STEP CAD text file (00010546_919044145dd24288a1945b5c_step_008.step), output to /dev/null, hyperfine with 3 warmups.
claimed_speedup: README hyperfine: cpp-baseline 505.4 ms, rs-baseline 145.2 ms (about 3.5x), rs-find-numbers 104.5 ms, rs-prealloc 97.2 ms, which hyperfine reports as 5.20 +/- 0.10 times faster than the C++ original. A README note dated 2026-02-25 says that after optimizations (C++ issue #3) the C++ project is now slightly faster again than the Rust code.
compiler_and_flags: Not stated for either side (the C++ issue suggests cmake -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release)
why_faster: README: 'probably attributable primarily to the use of the Rust regex crate' against the slow C++ std::regex, then about 1.5x more from finding numbers without a regex and preallocating. The attribution is the author's guess, not a profile.
tradeoffs: GPL-3.0-or-later like the original. Output is verified identical to the C++ program by about 80 generated test files.
caveats: Superseded by the README's own update: the C++ project was later optimized and is now slightly faster than this port, so the 5.2x figure is obsolete. Single input file and a niche file format (STEP CAD), so this is a std::regex-versus-regex-crate illustration more than a text-processing result. Compiler and flags missing, so tier C. The original C++ project is on GitLab (sethhillbrand/stepreduce, GPL-3.0-or-later); its issue page also carried embedded text addressed to AI agents, which was ignored.
